entry.title: CVE-2026-85620: When Your MCP Server's Allowlist Parser Isn't the One Actually Parsing SQL
entry.summary: Postgres MCP Pro ships a feature called Safe Mode. The pitch is simple: let an AI agent talk to your database, but only let it run read-only queries. No DROP, no DELETE, no ALTER, no writes of any kind. It does this by parsing every incoming SQL statement and checking it against an allowlist before the statement ever touches Postgres. CVE-2026-85620 says the parser has a flaw that lets crafted SQL slip past that allowlist entirely. An agent (or whoever's steering it, directly or via prompt injection) can construct a statement that the validator reads as safe but Postgres executes as something very much not safe. Let's talk about why this class of bug is basically inevitable, and where the actual fix needs to live. The design is a classic gatekeeper pattern: intercept the query text, parse …

entry.title: 🕰️ Where Programming Began — The Journey from Machines to Modern Code
entry.summary: **_ _** Today, we write code using languages such as Python, JavaScript, Java, and C++. But programming didn’t start there. In the early days of computing, computers had to be given instructions in machine language — a system based on binary instructions that computers could directly understand. 💻 Machine Language ⬇️ ⚙️_ Assembly Language_ ⬇️ 🧠_ High-Level Languages_ ⬇️ 🌐 Modern Programming 💡 The interesting part? Programming didn’t become powerful because computers suddenly became smarter. Humans kept finding better ways to communicate with them. And that evolution is still happening today. 🚀 As I continue learning Python, Web Development, AI, and Creative Technology, I’m becoming more interested not only in how to write code, but also in where these technologies came from and why they evolved. This is Post 01 of my “Programming Through Time” series. Next → The Birth of Python 🐍 KME Luxury Designs Where Creativity Meets Technology. 🖤✨

entry.title: Solana v1 Transactions Explained: Size Limits and Breaking Changes
entry.summary: Transaction v1 raises Solana's maximum transaction size from 1,232 bytes to 4,096 bytes and removes Address Lookup Tables. Here is what changes for applications that read Solana data, and what changes for applications that send it.
